Break
brāke
v. (rendering Hebrew shabar/parar, Greek klaō/luō)
From Saxon brecan, to break, cognate with Latin frango. Hebrew shabar is to break in pieces; parar, to break a covenant or frustrate a purpose — the same verb for smashing a vessel and for violating an oath, which is the Hebrew way of saying that a broken promise is a broken thing.

Biblical Definition

Scripture distinguishes sharply between the breaking God requires and the breaking He refuses to do. What He requires is the heart: “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise” (Psalm 51:17) — the one offering a sinner can bring that will not be turned away. What He refuses is the weak: “A bruised reed shall he not break, and smoking flax shall he not quench, till he send forth judgment unto victory” (Matthew 12:20) — a Messiah who does not finish off what is already damaged. What He does to the hard is another matter entirely: “Is not my word like as a fire? saith the LORD; and like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces?” (Jeremiah 23:29) — the same word that binds up a broken heart shatters a proud one. And the church's central act carries the word into worship: the first believers “continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers” (Acts 2:42), where the breaking of bread recalls a body broken deliberately for others. The doctrine is a single line: God breaks the proud with His word, refuses to break the bruised, receives the broken heart as sacrifice, and gives His own broken body as the ground of it all.

Webster 1828 Definition

To part by violence; to burst or shatter; to violate, as a covenant; to break bread. In Scripture, the broken and contrite heart God will not despise, the bruised reed He will not break, His word as a hammer that breaks the rock, and the breaking of bread in the church's steadfast practice.

expand to see more

BREAK, v.t. 1. To part or divide by force and violence; to sever; to burst; to shatter.

2. To violate, as a contract or promise; as, to break faith, to break a covenant.

3. To tame; to subdue; to make tractable; as, to break a horse or a stubborn will.

4. From Saxon brecan; Latin frango, fregi, to break.

5. In Scripture, a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise, Ps. 51; a bruised reed shall he not break, Matt. 12.

Key Scripture

Psalm 51:17 — "The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise."

Matthew 12:20 — "A bruised reed shall he not break, and smoking flax shall he not quench, till he send forth judgment unto victory."

Jeremiah 23:29 — "Is not my word like as a fire? saith the LORD; and like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces?"

Acts 2:42 — "And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers."

Modern Corruption

Brokenness is aestheticised into a mood of general woundedness that requires no repentance, so that a word Scripture reserves for contrition over sin is used for suffering in general.

expand to see more

“Brokenness” has become a favourite word in the modern church, and it has quietly changed meaning. In David's Psalm the broken spirit is a man who has sinned against God, been confronted by a prophet, and come to the end of his defences: against thee, thee only, have I sinned, and done this evil in thy sight. The brokenness now commonly described is a state of woundedness — the pain of what has been done to a person rather than sorrow for what he has done to God — and the two are not the same, however genuinely both may hurt. Scripture has abundant tenderness for the afflicted; the smoking flax is not quenched, and the Man of sorrows is acquainted with grief. But contrition is a specific thing, it names sin as sin, and it is the sacrifice God accepts. A church that speaks constantly of brokenness and rarely of repentance has kept the vocabulary and lost the doctrine.

The second matter is the misuse of Matthew 12:20 to forbid all severity. The bruised reed is not broken, and no faithful minister should ever break one — but the same Lord who spoke that word wove a scourge of small cords, called Herod a fox, and told the Pharisees they were whited sepulchres. Jeremiah 23:29 is the necessary companion text: God's word is a hammer that breaks the rock in pieces, and rocks are what proud hearts are. Discernment consists in knowing which is in front of you. To use the hammer on a bruised reed is cruelty; to offer a bruised reed's comfort to a rock is flattery, and it leaves the man unbroken and unsaved. The principle to recover is that both instruments are in Scripture and both belong to love.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shabar, to break in pieces; dakah, to crush or be contrite; parar, to break a covenant; Greek klaō, to break bread, and syntribō, to shatter.

expand to see more

Hebrew shabar (H7665) — to break, shatter, or rend; used of vessels, of bones, and of a broken heart (Psalm 34:18).

Hebrew dakah (H1794) — to crush, to be contrite; the root of the contrite heart in Psalm 51:17.

Hebrew parar (H6565) — to break or frustrate, especially a covenant (Genesis 17:14).

Greek klaō (G2806) — to break, used exclusively of breaking bread in the New Testament (Acts 2:42; 20:7).

Greek syntribō (G4937) — to break in pieces, to crush; “a bruised reed shall he not break” (Matthew 12:20).

Usage

"Of the sacrifice God accepts: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise (Psalm 51:17)."

"Of the tenderness of Messiah: A bruised reed shall he not break (Matthew 12:20)."

"Of the word that shatters pride: like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces (Jeremiah 23:29)."
